screens.title: Variables, Data Types, and Basic Operators
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we learn the building blocks every Python program uses. You will see what a variable is, how Python categorizes values into integers, floating-point numbers, strings, and booleans, and how operators let you perform arithmetic, make comparisons, and combine conditions. Understanding these basics will help you avoid common type errors, write clearer code, and prepare for tasks like reading user input and computing results. For example, when you convert a typed string from user input to a floating-point number, you create usable numeric values for calculations. By the end of the lesson you can reason about a variable’s current type, apply arithmetic and logical operators correctly, and convert types where necessary. Think about the small programs you write next: these foundations make everything predictable, safer, and easier to debug.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Variables are labeled storage. Data types determine what operations make sense. Operators act on values and return results whose type depends on the operands.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Variables & Types Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Variables and Types: Why they matter

Variables let your program remember values. Data types tell Python what operations are valid and how values behave. Operators let you compute, compare, and combine values to express program logic.

In this lesson
Declare variables, identify types, and use operators safely.
Coming up
Type conversion, operator categories, and the BMI example.
Why it matters
Avoid runtime errors and express precise calculations and decisions.
Explore Key Topics
Three focal topics you'll practice in this chapter to make code reliable and readable.
Visual Concept

Labeled boxes: value, type, operations

Static illustration
Example state
A box labeled user_age holds a whole number type; a box labeled welcome_text holds a sequence of characters. Operations read the type to decide what is allowed.
Quick start
Declare a name, assign a value, and let Python infer the type. Convert explicitly when you must combine incompatible types.
Starter topics
Integers
Floats
Strings

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to declare and initialize variables that follow Python naming rules, recognize and use the basic built-in data types, apply arithmetic, assignment, comparison, and logical operators correctly, and perform explicit type conversions when mixing types. Each objective targets a practical skill: naming and initialization keep code readable and prevent syntax errors; knowing data types prevents type errors and guides which operations are valid; operator fluency helps you compute values and make decisions; and safe casting allows you to convert user input into usable numbers and avoid runtime exceptions. For example, when reading text input that represents a number you will convert that text to a floating-point value before doing division to avoid a type error. We'll practice with short examples and a small BMI program that combines input, conversion, arithmetic, and formatted output. If you can explain why a ValueError happens when converting non-numeric text to a number, and correct the code to guard against it, you have met the conversion objective.

screens.title: What is a Variable? Dynamic typing in Python
screens.narratorSegment: A variable is a named storage location that holds a value. Think of it as a labeled box where the label is the variable name and the box contains a value and an internal type. Python is dynamically typed, which means the interpreter determines the type from the value you assign rather than from an explicit declaration. For instance, assigning the number thirty to a name called user_age makes that name refer to an integer value; assigning a sequence of characters to a name creates a string. This flexibility speeds up development but requires discipline: the variable's type can change if you later assign a different kind of value. A common misconception is that variables carry a fixed type like in some statically typed languages. In Python, the name is a reference and the object it points to has the type. This means you can reassign a different type to the same name, but doing so without careful intent can introduce bugs. Practice tip: use descriptive names and keep each variable focused on a single role in a small block of code. Example: use weight_kg for mass in kilograms and avoid reusing the same name for both a number and a text value in the same scope. Key takeaway: variables give names to values; types live with values, not names.

keyIdea.title: Variable definition
keyIdea.text: A variable is a name bound to a value; Python infers the value's type at assignment time.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › What is a Variable?
Definition

Variables as labeled storage

A name points to a value object. The object's type determines what operations are valid on it.

Explanation
  • Names are references; objects have types.
  • Assigning a new value changes the object the name refers to.
  • Dynamic typing makes prototyping faster but requires careful variable use.
Analogy
Think of names as sticky labels and values as the boxes beneath them. You can remove a label and stick it to a different box, but the box still has its contents.
Concrete examples
Number example
A name holding a whole number used for counting or index values.
Text example
A name holding descriptive text used for messages or labels.
Check your understanding
If you assign a string to a name previously used for a number, what problems could arise? Consider later code that expects arithmetic.
Key Takeaway

Names label values. Types belong to values, not to names. Keep variable roles consistent to avoid confusion.

screens.title: Python's common built-in types
screens.narratorSegment: Python offers several fundamental built-in types you'll use constantly. Integers represent whole numbers and support exact arithmetic for counting, indexing, and many logic decisions. Floating-point numbers represent real numbers with a decimal component and are useful for measurements and calculations; be aware they can exhibit tiny precision differences because of binary representation. Strings are immutable sequences of characters for text, and operations like concatenation create new string objects rather than modifying existing ones. Booleans represent truth values used in conditionals and logical combinations. A clear mental model is to view types by category: numeric types for math, sequence types for ordered collections, and truth types for control flow. Misconceptions to avoid include assuming floating-point operations are always exact, or expecting to change a string in place. When you design code, choose types that make your intent explicit: use integers when counting items, floats for measured quantities, strings for labels, and booleans for binary conditions. This will make your logic easier to validate and less prone to type-related errors. Python's common built-in types means int and float for numbers, str for text, bool for truth values — each has behaviors and constraints to guide correct use.. In practical terms, integers, floats, strings, and booleans — roles and behaviors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Common Data Types

Type hierarchy

Group types by their purpose to pick the right one for the job.

Numeric types
  • int: whole numbers, exact
  • float: decimal numbers, may have precision quirks
Text and truth
  • str: immutable text sequences
  • bool: True or False, used for logic
Practical note
Use the appropriate type for clarity: do not store numeric data as text unless you need formatting — convert only when necessary.
Common mistake
Trying to add text and a number without conversion leads to a TypeError. Always convert explicit types before mixing operations.
Quick reference
Integer
Whole numbers for counts and discrete math.
Float
Decimal numbers for measurement; watch precision.
String
Text data, immutable; concatenation makes new strings.
Boolean
True / False values used in conditions and logic.
Key Takeaway

Choose types to match the role: counting, measuring, labeling, or deciding.

screens.title: Strings and Immutability
screens.narratorSegment: Strings are sequences of characters used to represent text. In Python strings are immutable, which means once a string object is created its content cannot be changed in place. Operations that appear to modify a string, such as concatenation, actually create a new string object and bind it to a name. This matters for performance when building long strings in loops and for reasoning about your program's state. For concatenation, you can use the plus operator to join pieces of text or use formatted strings to combine values and text clearly. A common example is building a message that includes a numeric result: convert the number to text or use a formatted string to embed the value without manual casting. Avoid the mistake of assuming you can modify a character by assignment. If you need a mutable sequence of characters for in-place edits, consider using a list of characters and then joining it back into a string. Concrete example: combine a first name and last name into a full name using concatenation or a formatted template, and remember that each join operation produces a new string object.

keyIdea.title: String behavior
keyIdea.text: Strings are immutable. Concatenation and formatting create new string objects rather than changing existing ones.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Strings & Immutability

Strings are immutable

Any operation that seems to change a string actually builds a new one and assigns the name to it.

Practical patterns
  • Concatenate short pieces for readable code.
  • Use formatted strings to combine numbers and text cleanly.
  • For heavy repeated concatenation, collect pieces and join them once.
Common mistake
Trying to assign to a character index in a string will fail because strings cannot be changed directly.
Examples
# Build a welcome message by joining pieces
greeting = "Hello"
name = "Taylor"
welcome = greeting + " " + name
# Using formatted text to include a number
score = 95
result_text = f"Your score: {score}"
These create new strings rather than changing existing ones. Use list+join if you build very large text incrementally.
Key Takeaway

Treat text as immutable. Use formatting for clarity and list-join for heavy concatenation.

screens.title: Booleans and Logical Operators
screens.narratorSegment: Booleans express truth. They are the result of comparisons and logical expressions and drive the flow of programs through conditionals and loops. The three key logical operators are and, or, and not. The operator and returns True only when both operands are True; or returns True when at least one operand is True; not negates a truth value. A practical example: when checking whether a value falls within a valid range, use and to ensure both lower and upper bounds hold. When validating input where multiple acceptable formats exist, or can combine the checks. A common confusion is mixing bitwise operators with logical operators; for boolean logic use the named operators, not single-character bitwise symbols. Also, remember comparison operators produce boolean results and can be chained: a less than b less than c expresses two comparisons in a readable way. For clarity, favor parentheses when combining many logical conditions. Concrete scenario: determining if a user is eligible for a service only if they are over a minimum age and have accepted terms — use and to require both conditions. Final question to keep in mind: does the expression reflect the real-world requirement you want to enforce?

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Booleans & Logic

Logical operators

Use and, or, and not to combine boolean expressions into the rules your program enforces.

  • and: True only if both parts are True.
  • or: True if at least one part is True.
  • not: Reverses a boolean value.
Misconception
Using bitwise operators for logical checks can produce unexpected results; use logical operators for boolean logic.
Concrete scenario
Eligibility rule: a user is accepted if they are at least a minimum age and have confirmed terms. Model each requirement as a boolean and combine them with and to enforce both.
Key Takeaway

Booleans and logical operators let you express the rules that control program flow; keep expressions clear with parentheses.

screens.title: Variable Naming Conventions
screens.narratorSegment: Good variable names communicate a value's role. PEP 8 recommends using snake_case for variable names: all lowercase with words separated by underscores. Names must start with a letter or an underscore and may include numbers and additional underscores, but they cannot start with a digit. Use descriptive names like total_price or user_name instead of single letters except when a short name is conventional, such as i for a loop index. Avoid using reserved words that are part of Python's language. Leading underscores are commonly used to indicate internal or private variables in modules or classes. A common mistake is using names that shadow built-in functions or types, such as assigning a value to a name called list or str; this can break calls to those built-ins later in the same scope. When in doubt, prefer clarity over brevity: a self-descriptive name reduces the need for comments and simplifies debugging. Practice: refactor a small script, replacing terse names with descriptive snake_case identifiers and observe how quickly intent becomes clearer. Variable Naming Conventions means use snake_case; start with a letter or underscore; avoid leading digits and shadowing built-ins for clearer, safer code.. In practical terms, pep 8 style and safe naming rules for maintainable code. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use snake_case; start with a letter or underscore; avoid leading digits and shadowing built-ins for clearer, safer code.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Naming Conventions

Rules and recommendations

  • Use snake_case for variable names.
  • Start names with a letter or underscore; do not start with a digit.
  • Avoid naming a variable after built-in types or functions.
  • Prefer descriptive names for readability.
Common mistake
Using a name like list to hold your data shadows Python's list type and can cause confusing errors later.
Refactor example
Change a variable called x to total_count and see how the code reads more clearly. Use comments sparingly when names are descriptive enough.
Key Takeaway

Good naming prevents bugs and makes your intent explicit — prefer descriptive snake_case identifiers.

screens.title: Arithmetic Operators and Precedence
screens.narratorSegment: Arithmetic operators let you calculate values. Python supports addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, floor division, modulo, and exponentiation. Division always produces a floating-point result in modern Python. Floor division returns the integer part of a quotient, and modulo returns the remainder. Exponentiation raises one number to the power of another. Operator precedence follows familiar mathematical rules: parentheses first, then exponentiation, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction. A common error is assuming left-to-right evaluation will override precedence — use parentheses to make intent explicit. Another important detail is that mixed numeric types yield numeric results consistent with the most general type: combining integers and floats in an expression typically produces a float. For practical debugging, print intermediate results or use parentheses to ensure operations happen in the order you expect. Example: computing a weighted average uses multiplication and addition, so grouping terms with parentheses clarifies the calculation and avoids subtle precedence bugs. Arithmetic Operators and Precedence means use +, -, *, /, //, %, and **. apply parentheses to enforce the intended order of operations.. In practical terms, perform calculations and remember the order of operations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Arithmetic & Precedence

Operator list

  • Addition, subtraction, multiplication, division.
  • Floor division returns the integer quotient; modulo returns remainder.
  • Exponentiation raises to a power.
Precedence reminder
Parentheses, exponents, multiplication/division, addition/subtraction. Use parentheses to make calculations explicit.
Practical tip
When mixing ints and floats, expect a float result. Print intermediate values when debugging calculations.
Example calculations
# Evaluate with clear grouping
weighted = (10 + 5) * 2 / 3
floor_part = 10 // 3  # integer part of division
remainder = 10 % 3
Group operations to avoid ambiguity and ensure correct numeric types in results.
Key Takeaway

Remember precedence and type promotion rules: parentheses, then exponents, then multiply/divide, then add/subtract.

screens.title: Assignment and Compound Assignment Operators
screens.narratorSegment: Assignment gives a name a value. The basic assignment operator sets a name to whatever the right-hand expression produces. Compound assignment operators combine an operation with assignment, such as adding and reassigning in one step. For example, instead of writing a name equals name plus five, you can write name plus equals five to update the value in place conceptually. These compound forms exist for addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, modulo, and exponentiation. They improve concision and reduce the chance of typos when updating a variable based on its current value. A subtle point is that for mutable objects the compound operator may mutate the object, while for immutable objects it creates a new object and rebinds the name. For example, adding to a list with an extend-like operation changes the list in place, but adding to a number results in a new numeric object bound to the name. Keep intent clear when using compound assignments and avoid shadowing names that confuse the operation's meaning. Assignment and Compound Assignment Operators means use = to assign. use +=, -=, *=, /=, %=, **= to update concisely; understand how immutability affects results.. In practical terms, setting values and using shorthand updates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Comparison Operators and a Common Mistake
screens.narratorSegment: Comparison operators compare two values and always return a boolean. Use equality and inequality checks to test whether values match, and the relational operators to compare ordering. For example, equality returns True when two values are equal. Also be mindful of types when comparing; comparing different types may give unexpected results or always return False when types are incompatible. content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › BMI Calculator

Script structure

The following starter script shows the full flow: input, conversion, validation, calculation, and formatted output.

# bmi_calculator.py
print("--- BMI Calculator ---")
weight_str = input("Enter your weight in kilograms (e.g., 70.5): ")
height_str = input("Enter your height in meters (e.g., 1.75): ")
try:
  weight_kg = float(weight_str)
  height_m = float(height_str)
except ValueError:
  print("Error: Please enter valid numbers for weight and height.")
  exit()
if height_m <= 0:
  print("Error: Height cannot be zero or negative. Please enter a positive value.")
  exit()
bmi = weight_kg / (height_m ** 2)
print(f"Your calculated BMI is: {bmi:.2f}")
Exercise
Run the script with valid and invalid inputs, then add boolean range checks that classify the BMI and print simple True/False flags for overweight and healthy ranges.
Example outputs
Formatted weight and height lines and a BMI rounded to two decimals improve usability. Boolean checks show classification logic in action.
Key Takeaway

A single small script can exercise variables, types, operators, conversions, and conditionals together — a great test bed for learning.

In this chapter we learn the building blocks every Python program uses. You will see what a variable is, how Python categorizes values into integers, floating-point numbers, strings, and booleans, and how operators let you perform arithmetic, make comparisons, and combine conditions. Understanding these basics will help you avoid common type errors, write clearer code, and prepare for tasks like reading user input and computing results. For example, when you convert a typed string from user input to a floating-point number, you create usable numeric values for calculations. We will also cover naming conventions that make your code easier to read and maintain and the simple rules for type conversion so you can safely change a value from text to a number. By the end of the lesson you can reason about a variable’s current type, apply arithmetic and logical operators correctly, and convert types where necessary. Think about the small programs you write next: these foundations make everything predictable, safer, and easier to debug.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to declare and initialize variables that follow Python naming rules, recognize and use the basic built-in data types, apply arithmetic, assignment, comparison, and logical operators correctly, and perform explicit type conversions when mixing types. Each objective targets a practical skill: naming and initialization keep code readable and prevent syntax errors; knowing data types prevents type errors and guides which operations are valid; operator fluency helps you compute values and make decisions; and safe casting allows you to convert user input into usable numbers and avoid runtime exceptions. For example, when reading text input that represents a number you will convert that text to a floating-point value before doing division to avoid a type error. We'll practice with short examples and a small BMI program that combines input, conversion, arithmetic, and formatted output. If you can explain why a ValueError happens when converting non-numeric text to a number, and correct the code to guard against it, you have met the conversion objective.

These objectives are not just items to check off. Each one maps to a practice you should be able to perform. For declaring variables, show that you can pick a meaningful snake case name and initialize it with a value that Python will infer. For data types, be able to state the difference between a whole number and a floating-point value, explain string immutability, and identify boolean truth values. For operators, write expressions that use compound assignment to update variables and logical operators to combine conditions. For type conversion, convert a numeric-looking string into an integer or float and handle the error case gracefully. A simple test to prove mastery is to write a small script that reads text input, casts it to a number, performs arithmetic, and prints a formatted result. If you can also explain why mixing a number and a string without conversion leads to a TypeError, you have a practical grasp of the chapter's core ideas.

A variable is a named storage location that holds a value. Think of it as a labeled box where the label is the variable name and the box contains a value and an internal type. Python is dynamically typed, which means the interpreter determines the type from the value you assign rather than from an explicit declaration. For instance, assigning the number thirty to a name called user_age makes that name refer to an integer value; assigning a sequence of characters to a name creates a string. This flexibility speeds up development but requires discipline: the variable's type can change if you later assign a different kind of value. A common misconception is that variables carry a fixed type like in some statically typed languages. In Python, the name is a reference and the object it points to has the type. This means you can reassign a different type to the same name, but doing so without careful intent can introduce bugs. Practice tip: use descriptive names and keep each variable focused on a single role in a small block of code. Example: use weight_kg for mass in kilograms and avoid reusing the same name for both a number and a text value in the same scope. Key takeaway: variables give names to values; types live with values, not names.

Python offers several fundamental built-in types you'll use constantly. Integers represent whole numbers and support exact arithmetic for counting, indexing, and many logic decisions. Floating-point numbers represent real numbers with a decimal component and are useful for measurements and calculations; be aware they can exhibit tiny precision differences because of binary representation. Strings are immutable sequences of characters for text, and operations like concatenation create new string objects rather than modifying existing ones. Booleans represent truth values used in conditionals and logical combinations. A clear mental model is to view types by category: numeric types for math, sequence types for ordered collections, and truth types for control flow. Misconceptions to avoid include assuming floating-point operations are always exact, or expecting to change a string in place. When you design code, choose types that make your intent explicit: use integers when counting items, floats for measured quantities, strings for labels, and booleans for binary conditions. This will make your logic easier to validate and less prone to type-related errors. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Strings are sequences of characters used to represent text. In Python strings are immutable, which means once a string object is created its content cannot be changed in place. Operations that appear to modify a string, such as concatenation, actually create a new string object and bind it to a name. This matters for performance when building long strings in loops and for reasoning about your program's state. For concatenation, you can use the plus operator to join pieces of text or use formatted strings to combine values and text clearly. A common example is building a message that includes a numeric result: convert the number to text or use a formatted string to embed the value without manual casting. Avoid the mistake of assuming you can modify a character by assignment. If you need a mutable sequence of characters for in-place edits, consider using a list of characters and then joining it back into a string. Concrete example: combine a first name and last name into a full name using concatenation or a formatted template, and remember that each join operation produces a new string object.

Booleans express truth. They are the result of comparisons and logical expressions and drive the flow of programs through conditionals and loops. The three key logical operators are and, or, and not. The operator and returns True only when both operands are True; or returns True when at least one operand is True; not negates a truth value. A practical example: when checking whether a value falls within a valid range, use and to ensure both lower and upper bounds hold. When validating input where multiple acceptable formats exist, or can combine the checks. A common confusion is mixing bitwise operators with logical operators; for boolean logic use the named operators, not single-character bitwise symbols. Also, remember comparison operators produce boolean results and can be chained: a less than b less than c expresses two comparisons in a readable way. For clarity, favor parentheses when combining many logical conditions. Concrete scenario: determining if a user is eligible for a service only if they are over a minimum age and have accepted terms — use and to require both conditions. Final question to keep in mind: does the expression reflect the real-world requirement you want to enforce?

Good variable names communicate a value's role. PEP 8 recommends using snake_case for variable names: all lowercase with words separated by underscores. Names must start with a letter or an underscore and may include numbers and additional underscores, but they cannot start with a digit. When in doubt, prefer clarity over brevity: a self-descriptive name reduces the need for comments and simplifies debugging.
